title.narrative: Bridging the Gap: Enhancing SRHR Access and Justice in Somalia 2024-2026

description.narrative: Det övergripande målet med insatsen 'Bridging the Gap', är att stärka tillgång till sexuell och reproduktiv hälsa och rättigheter i somaliska lokalsamhällen.
The main aim of the project 'Bridging the Gap', is to enhance sexual and reproductive health and rights access and justice in Somali communities.

The project, Bridging the Gap: Enhancing SRHR Access and Justice in Somali Communities, has three outcome objectives.
Outcome 1: Women and girls in fragile contexts have improved awareness of and protection from gender-based violence (GBV) and improved access to sexual and reproductive health and rights services.
Outcome 2: Communities in project target locations embrace gender equality and SRHR rights, leading to reduced harmful gender norms through dialogue and behavior change.
Outcome 3: More resilient and inclusive health system, with sustainable SRHR services for adolescents supported by robust policy frameworks.

description.narrative:
1. Sexual Reproductive Health (SRH) Results in 2025:
Expanded access to integrated SRHR and GBV services: In 2025, 104,009 people (28,267 male and 75,742 female) including both host and internally displaced persons (IDPs) accessed integrated SRHR and GBV services across project-supported facilities.
Services provided included antenatal care, postnatal care, primary healthcare consultations, skilled deliveries, EmONC, post-abortion care, STI treatment, family planning, and GBV clinical care.
Strengthened health workforce capacity: Under the project, 179 frontline healthcare workers (141 women and 38 men) were trained on integrated SRHR and GBV clinical care, in collaboration with national and sub-national Ministries of Health. Training was reinforced through clinical attachments, mentorship, and joint supportive supervision, contributing to improved clinical quality and sustained service delivery.
Community engagement driving SRH service uptake and behavior change: In 2025, 17,191 community members (13,380 women and girls; 3,811 men and boys) from both IDP and host communities were reached through CHW-led outreach and dialogue. These activities increased awareness, reduced misconceptions around SRHR and GBV, and strengthened community trust in public health services.
Improved quality, readiness, and resilience of public health facilities: In 2025, the project supported the full rehabilitation of two public health facilities (Arif Health Centre in Mogadishu and Waaberi Health Centre in Dhusamareb) and provided targeted infrastructure upgrades to four additional facilities. These investments strengthened facility capacity to deliver safe, dignified SRHR and GBV services, improving service quality and patient experience.
Strengthened systems, emergency preparedness, and enabling environment: In 2025, the project supported the Federal Ministry of Health to finalize and launch Somalias FP2030 commitment, convene a national Maternal and Reproductive Health ecosystem dialogue, and provide technical support for finalizing Post-Abortion Care guidelines (ongoing). These efforts strengthened national leadership and coordination, improved policy and guidance for quality SRH service delivery, and laid the foundation for more sustainable and accessible reproductive health services.
Additionally, 19 health officials and partners (MISP trained) were trained on the Minimum Initial Service Package (MISP) for SRH, strengthening emergency SRH planning and establishing a national pool of trainers for MISP scale-up. VCAT training for providers and civil society actors also reduced stigma and promoted gender-equitable service delivery.
2. Protection Results in 2025: Community outreach and GBV awareness: In 2025, 207,848 community members (85,711 male and 122,137 female) from both IDP and host communities were reached through dialogues, awareness activities, and community-led initiatives addressing harmful gender norms. This contributed to increased GBV awareness, reduced acceptance of harmful practices, and stronger community support for gender-equitable behaviors.
Capacity building for community influencers: 88 religious leaders, elders, and community focal points (61 male and 27 female) were trained on gender norms methodologies, strengthening their ability to promote positive masculinities, rights-based SRHR messaging, and influence social norms.
GBV/SRHR messaging and media outreach: A total of 54,995 people (19,700 male and 35,295 female) received harmonized GBV/SRHR messaging through dialogues and media platforms, resulting in improved understanding of GBV risks, available services, and SRHR rights.
SASA! Together Start Phase implementation: The SASA! Together Start Phase was implemented in Galmudug with 50 participants (26 male and 24 female) and 8 community dialogues, helping communities reflect on power dynamics and challenge root causes of GBV and FGM.
Community outreach campaigns: A total of 144,053 individuals (62,517 male and 81,536 female) from both IDP and host communities were engaged through outreach campaigns, expanding protection messaging and increasing access to information for marginalized groups.
Strengthened legal and policy environment to end FGM: The project supported legislative progress, including the passage of Southwest States Anti- FGM law, ongoing advocacy for Galmudugs law, and the Federal FGM Bill reaching its first reading. A comprehensive FGM Legislative Guide (English & Somali) was developed and adopted by state and federal actors, improving the quality and coherence of legislative drafting and advocacy processes. This was reinforced through three legal seminars reaching 90 participants (64 male and 26 female), which strengthened stakeholder understanding of FGM legislation and enhanced public communication around legal reforms.
Increased public awareness and community demand for protection: A multiplatform media campaign on Anti-FGM legislation reached 2,000,134 people (972,018 male and 1,028,116 female), significantly raising awareness of rights and legal protections. This was complemented by targeted community outreach and messaging, which strengthened public understanding and support for ending FGM.
Main Challenges 1. Ongoing insecurity and access limitations: Persistent conflict, Al-Shabaab activity, and localized clan tensions continue to restrict movement, disrupt outreach, and complicate supply routes across key regions. This increases operational complexity and threatens continuity of service delivery. 2. Political instability and election-related disruption: Rising political tensions and public demonstrations ahead of the 2026 elections may cause sudden access restrictions, delays in field movements, and temporary service disruptions. 3. Severe drought and reduced humanitarian capacity due to funding cuts: Somalia experienced sustained drought pressures in 2025, with an estimated 3.4 million people in crisis-level acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above), driven by prolonged drought, high food prices, and conflict-related disruptions.
These conditions increased displacement and heightened vulnerability, especially among IDPs, pastoralist communities, women, and children. At the same time, reductions and suspensions in U.S. government funding significantly weakened humanitarian response capacity, reducing access to primary health care, maternal and child health services, immunization, and nutrition support for vulnerable populations.
